All analyses were performed in R (version 4.2.1) using the survival and survminer packages. Results Patient characteristics A total of 502 lung transplant recipients were included (240 with postoperative DVT and 262 without). Baseline characteristics were broadly comparable between groups (Supplementary Table 1). Pre-transplant VV-ECMO bridging was more frequent in the DVT group (12.9% vs. 8.4%), though this did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.11). Pulmonary arterial hypertension was less common among patients with DVT (5.0% vs. 10.3%, p = 0.03). Intraoperative parameters were similar, except for longer operative time in the DVT group (5.6 [4.6–7.4] vs. 5.1 [3.9–6.6] hours, p = 0.01). Postoperatively, DVT was associated with higher rates of PE (22.5% vs. 5.0%, p < 0.0001), AKI (p = 0.009), and PGD grade 3 (p = 0.016), as well as greater resource use including hemodialysis after discharge, longer hospital stay, and more frequent post- VV-ECMO utilization (all p ≤ 0.010). Survival outcomes Kaplan–Meier analysis demonstrated significantly lower overall survival among patients with DVT compared to those without DVT (log-rank p < 0.001; HR 2.19, 95% CI 1.49–3.23; Fig. ). One-, three-, and five-year survival was 83.8%, 63.8%, and 46.9% in the DVT group versus 92.4%, 80.3%, and 77.4% without DVT. The DVT cohort showed a clear separation of survival curves early after transplantation, and the difference persisted throughout the observation period. Impact of VV-ECMO use on clinical characteristics in the DVT cohort Among the 240 patients with postoperative DVT, 31 (12.9%) were bridged with pre-transplant VV-ECMO (Supplementary Table 2). Compared with DVT patients without preoperative ECMO, VV-ECMO–bridged patients were younger and underwent more complex operations, with longer operative time and substantially higher transfusion requirements. Postoperatively, they had higher rates of anticoagulation use, PGD grade 3, and dialysis, and experienced prolonged ventilator support and hospitalization (all p < 0.05). Distribution of DVT locations according to VV-ECMO use Among patients who developed DVT within 14 days, upper-extremity (UE) DVTs were more frequent in the pre-operative VV-ECMO group than in the non- VV-ECMO group (53.3% [8/15] vs. 23.5% [19/81]; p = 0.03). In contrast, the proportions of lower-extremity DVT above the knee (20.0% vs. 23.5%; p = 1.00) and below the knee (40.0% vs. 43.2%; p = 1.00), as well as neck-vein thrombosis (26.7% vs. 45.7%; p = 0.26), did not differ significantly between groups. Within each anatomical stratum, rates of therapeutic anticoagulation were similar in VV-ECMO and non- VV-ECMO patients (Table , Supplementary Table 3). Risk factors for postoperative DVT Univariate logistic regression identified several perioperative factors associated with the development of DVT after lung transplantation (Table ). Among intraoperative parameters, longer operative time was significantly associated with an increased risk of DVT (odds ratio [OR] = 1.18, 95% CI 1.08–1.29, p < 0.001). Postoperative AKI (OR = 1.60, 95% CI 1.13–2.28, p = 0.009), PGD grade 3 (OR = 1.88, 95% CI 1.13–3.15, p = 0.02), and post- VV-ECMO use (OR = 2.08, 95% CI 1.21–3.64, p = 0.009) were also significantly correlated with DVT occurrence. Among preoperative variables, PAH showed a negative association with DVT risk (OR = 0.42, 95% CI 0.19–0.88, p = 0.03). On multivariate logistic regression, operative time remained an independent predictor of DVT (OR = 1.18, 95% CI 1.07–1.31, p < 0.001). In contrast, preoperative PAH continued to demonstrate a protective association (OR = 0.41, 95% CI 0.19–0.83, p = 0.02). Although postoperative AKI (OR = 1.43, 95% CI 0.98–2.08, p = 0.06) showed a trend toward significance, it did not reach statistical significance in the multivariate model. Other perioperative factors, including preoperative VV-ECMO bridging, post- VV-ECMO use, and PGD grade 3, were not independently associated with DVT after adjustment for confounders. Impact of VV-ECMO use on DVT-free survival The cumulative DVT-free survival of all 502 lung transplant recipients is shown in Fig. A. The majority of DVT events occurred within the early postoperative period, with the survival curve plateauing after approximately 1,000 days. Patients bridged to transplantation with VV-ECMO demonstrated significantly lower DVT-free survival compared with those without preoperative VV-ECMO support (log-rank p = 0.030; Fig. B). VV-ECMO–bridged subgroup analysis Among VV-ECMO–bridged lung transplant recipients (n = 53), 31 developed postoperative DVT and 22 did not. Baseline and intraoperative characteristics were largely comparable between groups; however, patients who developed DVT had longer time on the waitlist and longer VV-ECMO bridge duration (Table ). Postoperative outcomes were also broadly similar, although PE occurred numerically more often in the DVT group (22.6% vs. 4.5%), without reaching statistical significance in this small subgroup (Table ). Baseline and intraoperative characteristics were largely comparable between groups; however, patients who developed DVT had longer time on the waitlist and longer VV-ECMO bridge duration (Table ). Postoperative outcomes were also broadly similar, although PE occurred numerically more often in the DVT group (22.6% vs. 4.5%), without reaching statistical significance in this small subgroup (Table ). We further examined the relationship between anticoagulation exposure and subsequent PE within the VV-ECMO cohort (Supplementary Fig. 1). Case-level review confirmed that no patients-initiated anticoagulation after PE diagnosis; anticoagulation exposure, when present, occurred before the PE event (Supplementary Table 4). Association between VV-ECMO Use, anticoagulation, and thromboembolic events In the analysis of anticoagulation patterns stratified by VV-ECMO status, DVT, and PE (Supplementary Table 5), anticoagulation therapy was administered more frequently in patients who developed thromboembolic complications and in those requiring VV-ECMO support. Among patients supported with preoperative VV-ECMO, anticoagulation was used in 50.0% of those with both DVT and PE and 64.0% of those with DVT alone, compared with 68.0% and 35.3%, respectively, in patients without VV-ECMO. Overall, anticoagulation utilization was lowest among patients without DVT or PE who did not require VV-ECMO. In the subgroup of patients who developed DVT, the relationship between anticoagulation and PE was further examined (Supplementary Fig. 2). The incidence of PE was significantly higher in patients who received anticoagulation than in those who did not (49/180 (27.2%) vs. 5/60 (8.3%), p = 0.002). Consistent with this finding, Kaplan–Meier analysis of PE-free survival (Supplementary Fig. 3) showed that patients receiving anticoagulation had significantly worse PE-free survival compared with those not receiving anticoagulation (log-rank p = 0.0053). The difference between the two groups became evident early after transplantation and persisted throughout follow-up. Relationship between anticoagulation and hemorrhagic complications To assess whether anticoagulation increased the risk of bleeding, hemothorax and hematoma-free survival was compared between patients who did and did not receive anticoagulation (Supplementary Fig. 4). There was no significant difference in hemothorax/hematoma-free survival between the two groups (log-rank p = 0.367). Both curves showed a modest early decline, but long-term survival remained comparable thereafter. Discussion In this single-center retrospective analysis, we identified a high incidence of post-transplant DVT among lung transplant recipients and demonstrated that DVT was associated with significantly worse postoperative outcomes, including higher rates of pulmonary embolism, acute kidney injury, PGD grade 3, and prolonged hospitalization. Importantly, overall survival was significantly reduced in recipients who developed DVT compared with those who did not. Preoperative VV-ECMO was not independently associated with postoperative DVT after multivariable adjustment; however, VV-ECMO bridging identified a high-risk clinical phenotype, characterized by greater perioperative complexity and higher early post-transplant thrombotic hazard, supporting the need for intensified early surveillance in this subgroup. Together, these findings underscore the clinical relevance of thromboembolic complications in lung transplantation and highlight the need for optimized anticoagulation strategies, particularly for patients requiring VV-ECMO support as a bridge to transplant. Notably, VV-ECMO bridging has emerged as a standard practice for patients with acute or rapidly progressive respiratory failure awaiting transplantation [ , – ]. Although it improves pretransplant survival, VV-ECMO introduces complex hemostatic alterations due to continuous exposure of blood to artificial surfaces, systemic inflammation, and fluctuating anticoagulation levels [ ]. Prior investigations have shown that DVT can occur in up to 40–50% of VV-ECMO-supported patients [ – ]. In our study, 12.9% of patients with post-transplant DVT had preoperative VV-ECMO support, and these patients exhibited more severe perioperative coagulopathy, longer operative times, and higher transfusion requirements. The association between DVT and adverse outcomes may be multifactorial. One can be that the observed association between DVT and acute kidney injury suggests a broader prothrombotic systemic milieu, possibly mediated by venous congestion, systemic inflammation, and impaired microcirculation [ ]. The observed inverse association between preoperative PAH and post-transplant DVT deserves cautious interpretation. Although PAH was independently associated with lower odds of DVT in our multivariable model, the number of PAH recipients in this cohort was relatively small, and this finding may be susceptible to residual confounding or model instability. Clinically, several non-mutually exclusive explanations are possible. PAH recipients may undergo more standardized hemodynamic management and early postoperative monitoring, and their perioperative care pathways may differ with respect to fluid management, mobilization, and thresholds for initiating pharmacologic prophylaxis or therapeutic anticoagulation. In addition, recipient selection and underlying disease biology may differ from ILD/COPD populations in ways that are not fully captured by the available covariates. Therefore, this association should be considered hypothesis-generating and warrants validation in larger, multicenter datasets with more granular perioperative management variables. The relationship between anticoagulation therapy and pulmonary embolism warrants special consideration. The higher rate of PE among anticoagulated patients likely reflects treatment bias—patients with more extensive or

standardized hemodynamic management and early postoperative monitoring, and their perioperative care pathways may differ with respect to fluid management, mobilization, and thresholds for initiating pharmacologic prophylaxis or therapeutic anticoagulation. In addition, recipient selection and underlying disease biology may differ from ILD/COPD populations in ways that are not fully captured by the available covariates. Therefore, this association should be considered hypothesis-generating and warrants validation in larger, multicenter datasets with more granular perioperative management variables. The relationship between anticoagulation therapy and pulmonary embolism warrants special consideration. The higher rate of PE among anticoagulated patients likely reflects treatment bias—patients with more extensive or symptomatic DVT were preferentially anticoagulated rather than anticoagulation being causative of PE. Importantly, anticoagulation was not associated with a higher incidence of hemorrhagic complications, suggesting that appropriately titrated therapy may be safe even in the early post-transplant setting. This finding is clinically relevant, as concerns about postoperative bleeding often delay or limit anticoagulation initiation in this population. Lastly, comparing VV-ECMO bridge and non VV-ECMO bridge group, there was no significant difference in the day of development DVT after lung transplant. Therefore, screening timing of DVT could be similar in both groups. Consistent with Fig. b, the VV-ECMO–bridged cohort shows a higher early hazard of DVT than non-bridged recipients, underscoring the need for intensified early postoperative surveillance and a lower threshold for diagnostic imaging. These results emphasize the need for proactive DVT surveillance and individualized anticoagulation management in VV- ECMO bridged lung transplant recipients. Early duplex ultrasonography should be considered for all high-risk patients, especially those with prolonged operative times or early signs of PGD or renal dysfunction. Our findings suggest that postoperative DVT is not a benign event and warrants prompt recognition and intervention. Furthermore, institutional standardization of perioperative anticoagulation protocols—including timing of reinitiation, target therapeutic ranges, and use of anti-Xa monitoring—may help mitigate variability and improve outcomes. Future multicenter studies are needed to determine optimal anticoagulation intensity and timing, balancing thrombosis prevention with bleeding risk in this fragile patient group. This study has several limitations. Its retrospective design introduces potential for selection bias and unmeasured confounding. The analysis was performed at a single high-volume transplant center, which may limit generalizability to other institutions with different VV-ECMO practices or anticoagulation protocols. Duplex ultrasonography was not performed uniformly across all patients, raising the possibility of underdiagnosis of asymptomatic DVT. In addition, surveillance bias is possible, because VV-ECMO–bridged or otherwise higher-acuity patients may have been more likely to undergo diagnostic imaging, potentially increasing DVT detection independent of true incidence. Because the frequency of duplex ultrasonography was not available in a standardized manner, we were unable to quantify imaging intensity by subgroup, and this limitation should be considered when interpreting group comparisons. Additionally, information on long-term anticoagulation adherence and PE severity was limited. Because anticoagulation exposure was analyzed largely as a binary variable, our findings may be subject to time-dependent confounding and reverse causation if anticoagulation was initiated in response to evolving clinical suspicion or diagnosis of thromboembolic events; therefore, the observed association between anticoagulation and PE should not be interpreted as causal. Although case-level review in the VV-ECMO–bridged cohort confirmed that anticoagulation preceded PE diagnosis, residual time-dependent bias cannot be excluded in the overall cohort. Nonetheless, the large sample size, standardized institutional protocols, and long follow-up period strengthen the validity of our findings. Conclusion In summary, post-transplant DVT represents a frequent and clinically significant complication among lung transplant recipients, particularly those bridged with VV-ECMO. DVT is associated with increased postoperative morbidity, prolonged hospitalization, and reduced survival. Preoperative VV-ECMO support identifies a subgroup with higher hemostatic complexity and greater susceptibility to thromboembolic events. Our findings highlight the need for vigilant DVT surveillance and optimization of perioperative anticoagulation strategies to improve post-transplant outcomes in this high-risk population. While anticoagulation management is central to preventing thrombosis, strategies differ widely among institutions, reflecting uncertainty regarding optimal timing and intensity of therapy resumption following transplantation. International consensus guidance has increasingly standardized key aspects of VV-ECMO management, including patient selection, cannulation strategy, and circuit management. However, anticoagulation practices remain heterogeneous across centers, with substantial inter-institutional variation in monitoring assays (ACT, aPTT, anti-Xa) and target ranges [ , ]. Balancing the risks of postoperative bleeding, graft dysfunction, and thrombosis remains one of the most challenging aspects of peri-transplant management. Consequently, critical gaps persist in understanding the incidence, risk factors, and clinical consequences of post-transplant DVT in VV-ECMO-bridged recipients. It remains unclear whether DVT after transplantation influences early recovery, intensive care unit (ICU) stay, mechanical ventilation duration, or longer-term outcomes such as graft function and survival. Similarly, the impact of varying anticoagulation strategies on the development and progression of DVT in this population has not been defined. Addressing these questions is essential, as identification of modifiable factors could directly inform perioperative management and improve both short- and long-term transplant outcomes. At our center, VV-ECMO bridging is routinely managed using a heparin-sparing approach in which continuous systemic anticoagulation is withheld unless clinically indicated such as DVT/PE, an approach that has been reported to be feasible without excess major thrombotic complications in selected VV-ECMO patients [ ]. In this retrospective single-center study, the primary objective was to define the incidence and clinical impact of post-transplant DVT in the overall lung transplant cohort. Secondary objectives were to (i) characterize DVT risk and early anatomic distribution in recipients bridged with preoperative VV-ECMO and (ii) compare DVT-free survival by VV-ECMO bridging status. Exploratory analyses evaluated anticoagulation patterns in relation to thromboembolic and hemorrhagic outcomes. Together, these analyses aim to inform peri-transplant thrombosis surveillance and anticoagulation decision-making. Patients and methods Study design This retrospective single-center study was conducted at Northwestern University Medical Center in Chicago, Illinois, USA. The study protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Northwestern University (STU00207250 and STU00213616). The need for informed consent was waived due to the retrospective nature of the study. Adult patients (≥ 18 years old) who underwent lung transplantation at Northwestern University between January 2018 and April 2025 were eligible for inclusion. Patients who received multiorgan transplants or underwent retransplantation were excluded. Clinical data were retrieved from institutional electronic medical records and entered into a prospectively maintained lung transplant database. This study focused on patients bridged to lung transplantation with preoperative VV-ECMO. Patients supported with veno-arterial ECMO (VA-ECMO) or VAV-ECMO as a preoperative bridge were excluded from the analytic cohort. Intraoperative VA-ECMO use for cardiopulmonary support during transplantation was recorded as an operative variable and does not represent the preoperative bridging ECMO modality. Patients supported with veno-arterial ECMO (VA-ECMO) or VAV-ECMO as a preoperative bridge were excluded from the analytic cohort. Intraoperative VA-ECMO use for cardiopulmonary support during transplantation was recorded as an operative variable and does not represent the preoperative bridging ECMO modality. Comprehensive data were collected on recipient demographics, baseline comorbidities, donor characteristics, preoperative laboratory results, and intraoperative variables including ischemic time, use and duration of VV-ECMO support, and transfusion requirements. Postoperative outcomes were also recorded, including duration of mechanical ventilation, intensive care unit (ICU) length of stay, hospital stay, and early complications. The primary outcome was development of post-transplant DVT. The primary analysis evaluated the association of DVT with postoperative outcomes and survival; secondary analyses evaluated DVT patterns and outcomes in the VV-ECMO–bridged subgroup. Secondary outcomes included ICU length of stay, postoperative bleeding events, need for reoperation, 30-day and 1-year mortality, and overall survival. The association between post-transplant DVT and clinical outcomes was analyzed. Perioperative VV-ECMO indication criteria Prior to lung transplantation, all intubated patients were treated by a multidisciplinary team in accordance with the guidelines of the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute’s ARDS Network [ ]. Indications for VV-ECMO evaluation included refractory hypoxemia with PaO 2 less than 55 mmHg, pulse oximetry oxygen saturation less than 88%, and pH level less than 7.2. Patients were evaluated with lung-protective mechanical ventilation with a plateau pressure of less than 35 mmHg, neuromuscular blockade, and prone positioning, according to recommendations from the Extracorporeal Life Support Organization [ ]. Anticoagulation during VV-ECMO support Patients did not receive continuous anticoagulation unless there was a specific indication, such as deep venous thrombosis or pulmonary embolism, and there was no monitoring of bleeding parameters, such as activated clotting time or activated partial thromboplastin time. All patients who were not receiving continuous systemic anticoagulation received 5,000 U of subcutaneous unfractionated heparin every 8 h as a prophylactic dose to prevent deep venous thrombosis. VV-ECMO flow was maintained at a minimum of 3.0–3.5 L/min, consistent with our recent reports, to reduce thrombotic complications in the VV-ECMO circuit [ , – ]. In this study, “anticoagulation use” was defined as receipt of systemic anticoagulation at any time after lung transplantation (e.g., intravenous unfractionated heparin infusion and/or subsequent transition to an oral anticoagulant), initiated for clinical indications such as DVT or PE at the discretion of the treating team. DVT surveillance and imaging Venous duplex ultrasonography for DVT assessment was not performed as routine screening after lung transplantation at our institution. Instead, duplex imaging was obtained only when clinically indicated based on symptoms or provider concern (e.g., limb swelling or pain, unexplained hypoxemia, or other findings suggestive of thromboembolism) [ ]. Because duplex examinations were ordered on an as-needed basis, the number and timing of duplex studies were not captured in a uniform structured format in the dataset and could not be reliably quantified across patient subgroups. Definition of complication Primary graft dysfunction (PGD) PGD was defined based on the ISHLT guideline and graded by PaO2/FiO2 ratio as follows; Grade 1: PaO2/FiO2 ratio > 300; Grade 2: PaO2/FiO2 ratio is 200–300; Grade 3: PaO2/FiO2 ratio < 200 [ ]. Chronic lung allograft dysfunction (CLAD) CLAD is defined as a sustained (at least 3 months) decline in the forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV₁) of at least 20% from the post-transplant baseline, in the absence of other reversible causes. CLAD is further sub-classified into phenotypes such as bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome (BOS) and restrictive allograft syndrome (RAS) based on clinical, radiologic, and physiologic criteria [ ]. Acute kidney injury (AKI) AKI was defined using the Risk, Failure, Loss of kidney function, and End-stage kidney disease classification [ ]. Statistical analysis Continuous variables were expressed as median (interquartile range, IQR) and compared using the Mann–Whitney U test. Categorical variables were expressed as counts and percentages and compared using Fisher’s exact test. Survival curves were estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method and compared using the log-rank test. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses were used to identify predictors of post-transplant DVT, whereas Cox proportional hazards analysis was used to evaluate the effect of DVT on mortality. Variables with a p -value < 0.10 in univariate analysis were included in multivariate models. Statistical significance was defined as p < 0.05. All analyses were performed in R (version 4.2.1) using the survival and survminer packages. Results Patient characteristics A total of 502 lung transplant recipients were included (240 with postoperative DVT and 262 without). Baseline characteristics were broadly comparable between groups (Supplementary Table 1). Pre-transplant VV-ECMO bridging was more frequent in the DVT group (12.9% vs. 8.4%), though this did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.11). Pulmonary arterial hypertension was less common among patients with DVT (5.0% vs. 10.3%, p = 0.03). Intraoperative parameters were similar, except for longer operative time in the DVT group (5.6 [4.6–7.4] vs. 5.1 [3.9–6.6] hours, p = 0.01). Postoperatively, DVT was associated with higher rates of PE (22.5% vs. 5.0%, p < 0.0001), AKI (p = 0.009), and PGD grade 3 (p = 0.016), as well as greater resource use including hemodialysis after discharge, longer hospital stay, and more frequent post- VV-ECMO utilization (all p ≤ 0.010). Survival outcomes Kaplan–Meier analysis demonstrated significantly lower overall survival among patients with DVT compared to those without DVT (log-rank p < 0.001; HR 2.19, 95% CI 1.49–3.23; Fig. ). One-, three-, and five-year survival was 83.8%, 63.8%, and 46.9% in the DVT group versus 92.4%, 80.3%, and 77.4% without DVT. The DVT cohort showed a clear separation of survival curves early after transplantation, and the difference persisted throughout the observation period. Impact of VV-ECMO use on clinical characteristics in the DVT cohort Among the 240 patients with postoperative DVT, 31 (12.9%) were bridged with pre-transplant VV-ECMO (Supplementary Table 2). Compared with DVT patients without preoperative ECMO, VV-ECMO–bridged patients were younger and underwent more complex operations, with longer operative time and substantially higher transfusion requirements. Postoperatively, they had higher rates of anticoagulation use, PGD grade 3, and dialysis, and experienced prolonged ventilator support and hospitalization (all p < 0.05). Distribution of DVT locations according to VV-ECMO use Among patients who developed DVT within 14 days, upper-extremity (UE) DVTs were more frequent in the pre-operative VV-ECMO group than in the non- VV-ECMO group (53.3% [8/15] vs. 23.5% [19/81]; p = 0.03). In contrast, the proportions of lower-extremity DVT above the knee (20.0% vs. 23.5%; p = 1.00) and below the knee (40.0% vs. 43.2%; p = 1.00), as well as neck-vein thrombosis (26.7% vs. 45.7%; p = 0.26), did not differ significantly between groups. Within each anatomical stratum, rates of therapeutic anticoagulation were similar in VV-ECMO and non- VV-ECMO patients (Table , Supplementary Table 3). Risk factors for postoperative DVT Univariate logistic regression identified several perioperative factors associated with the development of DVT after lung transplantation (Table ). Among intraoperative parameters, longer operative time was significantly associated with an increased risk of DVT (odds ratio [OR] = 1.18, 95% CI 1.08–1.29, p < 0.001). Postoperative AKI (OR = 1.60, 95% CI 1.13–2.28, p = 0.009), PGD grade 3 (OR = 1.88, 95% CI 1.13–3.15, p = 0.02), and post- VV-ECMO use (OR = 2.08, 95% CI 1.21–3.64, p = 0.009) were also significantly correlated with DVT occurrence. Among preoperative variables, PAH showed a negative association with DVT risk (OR = 0.42, 95% CI 0.19–0.88, p = 0.03). On multivariate logistic regression, operative time remained an independent predictor of DVT (OR = 1.18, 95% CI 1.07–1.31, p < 0.001). In contrast, preoperative PAH continued to demonstrate a protective association (OR = 0.41, 95% CI 0.19–0.83, p = 0.02). Although postoperative AKI (OR = 1.43, 95% CI 0.98–2.08, p = 0.06) showed a trend toward significance, it did not reach statistical significance in the multivariate model. Other perioperative factors, including preoperative VV-ECMO bridging, post- VV-ECMO use, and PGD grade 3, were not independently associated with DVT after adjustment for confounders. Impact of VV-ECMO use on DVT-free survival The cumulative DVT-free survival of all 502 lung transplant recipients is shown in Fig. A. The majority of DVT events occurred within the early postoperative period, with the survival curve plateauing after approximately 1,000 days. Patients bridged to transplantation with VV-ECMO demonstrated significantly lower DVT-free survival compared with those without preoperative VV-ECMO support (log-rank p = 0.030; Fig. B). VV-ECMO–bridged subgroup analysis Among VV-ECMO–bridged lung transplant recipients (n = 53), 31 developed postoperative DVT and 22 did not. Baseline and intraoperative characteristics were largely comparable between groups; however, patients who developed DVT had longer time on the waitlist and longer VV-ECMO bridge duration (Table ). Postoperative outcomes were also broadly similar, although PE occurred numerically more often in the DVT group (22.6% vs. 4.5%), without reaching statistical significance in this small subgroup (Table ). Baseline and intraoperative characteristics were largely comparable between groups; however, patients who developed DVT had longer time on the waitlist and longer VV-ECMO bridge duration (Table ). Postoperative outcomes were also broadly similar, although PE occurred numerically more often in the DVT group (22.6% vs. 4.5%), without reaching statistical significance in this small subgroup (Table ). We further examined the relationship between anticoagulation exposure and subsequent PE within the VV-ECMO cohort (Supplementary Fig. 1). Case-level review confirmed that no patients-initiated anticoagulation after PE diagnosis; anticoagulation exposure, when present, occurred before the PE event (Supplementary Table 4). Association between VV-ECMO Use, anticoagulation, and thromboembolic events In the analysis of anticoagulation patterns stratified by VV-ECMO status, DVT, and PE (Supplementary Table 5), anticoagulation therapy was administered more frequently in patients who developed thromboembolic complications and in those requiring VV-ECMO support. Among patients supported with preoperative VV-ECMO, anticoagulation was used in 50.0% of those with both DVT and PE and 64.0% of those with DVT alone, compared with 68.0% and 35.3%, respectively, in patients without VV-ECMO. Overall, anticoagulation utilization was lowest among patients without DVT or PE who did not require VV-ECMO. In the subgroup of patients who developed DVT, the relationship between anticoagulation and PE was further examined (Supplementary Fig. 2). The incidence of PE was significantly higher in patients who received anticoagulation than in those who did not (49/180 (27.2%) vs. 5/60 (8.3%), p = 0.002). Consistent with this finding, Kaplan–Meier analysis of PE-free survival (Supplementary Fig. 3) showed that patients receiving anticoagulation had significantly worse PE-free survival compared with those not receiving anticoagulation (log-rank p = 0.0053). The difference between the two groups became evident early after transplantation and persisted throughout follow-up. Relationship between anticoagulation and hemorrhagic complications To assess whether anticoagulation increased the risk of bleeding, hemothorax and hematoma-free survival was compared between patients who did and did not receive anticoagulation (Supplementary Fig. 4). There was no significant difference in hemothorax/hematoma-free survival between the two groups (log-rank p = 0.367). Both curves showed a modest early decline, but long-term survival remained comparable thereafter. Discussion In this single-center retrospective analysis, we identified a high incidence of post-transplant DVT among lung transplant recipients and demonstrated that DVT was associated with significantly worse postoperative outcomes, including higher rates of pulmonary embolism, acute kidney injury, PGD grade 3, and prolonged hospitalization. Importantly, overall survival was significantly reduced in recipients who developed DVT compared with those who did not. Preoperative VV-ECMO was not independently associated with postoperative DVT after multivariable adjustment; however, VV-ECMO bridging identified a high-risk clinical phenotype, characterized by greater perioperative complexity and higher early post-transplant thrombotic hazard, supporting the need for intensified early surveillance in this subgroup. Together, these findings underscore the clinical relevance of thromboembolic complications in lung transplantation and highlight the need for optimized anticoagulation strategies, particularly for patients requiring VV-ECMO support as a bridge to transplant. Notably, VV-ECMO bridging has emerged as a standard practice for patients with acute or rapidly progressive respiratory failure awaiting transplantation [ , – ]. Although it improves pretransplant survival, VV-ECMO introduces complex hemostatic alterations due to continuous exposure of blood to artificial surfaces, systemic inflammation, and fluctuating anticoagulation levels [ ]. Prior investigations have shown that DVT can occur in up to 40–50% of VV-ECMO-supported patients [ – ]. In our study, 12.9% of patients with post-transplant DVT had preoperative VV-ECMO support, and these patients exhibited more severe perioperative coagulopathy, longer operative times, and higher transfusion requirements. The association between DVT and adverse outcomes may be multifactorial. One can be that the observed association between DVT and acute kidney injury suggests a broader prothrombotic systemic milieu, possibly mediated by venous congestion, systemic inflammation, and impaired microcirculation [ ]. The observed inverse association between preoperative PAH and post-transplant DVT deserves cautious interpretation. Although PAH was independently associated with lower odds of DVT in our multivariable model, the number of PAH recipients in this cohort was relatively small, and this finding may be susceptible to residual confounding or model instability. Clinically, several non-mutually exclusive explanations are possible. PAH recipients may undergo more standardized hemodynamic management and early postoperative monitoring, and their perioperative care pathways may differ with respect to fluid management, mobilization, and thresholds for initiating pharmacologic prophylaxis or therapeutic anticoagulation. In addition, recipient selection and underlying disease biology may differ from ILD/COPD populations in ways that are not fully captured by the available covariates. Therefore, this association should be considered hypothesis-generating and warrants validation in larger, multicenter datasets with more granular perioperative management variables. The relationship between anticoagulation therapy and pulmonary embolism warrants special consideration. The higher rate of PE among anticoagulated patients likely reflects treatment bias—patients with more extensive or

standardized hemodynamic management and early postoperative monitoring, and their perioperative care pathways may differ with respect to fluid management, mobilization, and thresholds for initiating pharmacologic prophylaxis or therapeutic anticoagulation. In addition, recipient selection and underlying disease biology may differ from ILD/COPD populations in ways that are not fully captured by the available covariates. Therefore, this association should be considered hypothesis-generating and warrants validation in larger, multicenter datasets with more granular perioperative management variables. The relationship between anticoagulation therapy and pulmonary embolism warrants special consideration. The higher rate of PE among anticoagulated patients likely reflects treatment bias—patients with more extensive or symptomatic DVT were preferentially anticoagulated rather than anticoagulation being causative of PE. Importantly, anticoagulation was not associated with a higher incidence of hemorrhagic complications, suggesting that appropriately titrated therapy may be safe even in the early post-transplant setting. This finding is clinically relevant, as concerns about postoperative bleeding often delay or limit anticoagulation initiation in this population. Lastly, comparing VV-ECMO bridge and non VV-ECMO bridge group, there was no significant difference in the day of development DVT after lung transplant. Therefore, screening timing of DVT could be similar in both groups. Consistent with Fig. b, the VV-ECMO–bridged cohort shows a higher early hazard of DVT than non-bridged recipients, underscoring the need for intensified early postoperative surveillance and a lower threshold for diagnostic imaging. These results emphasize the need for proactive DVT surveillance and individualized anticoagulation management in VV- ECMO bridged lung transplant recipients. Early duplex ultrasonography should be considered for all high-risk patients, especially those with prolonged operative times or early signs of PGD or renal dysfunction. Our findings suggest that postoperative DVT is not a benign event and warrants prompt recognition and intervention. Furthermore, institutional standardization of perioperative anticoagulation protocols—including timing of reinitiation, target therapeutic ranges, and use of anti-Xa monitoring—may help mitigate variability and improve outcomes. Future multicenter studies are needed to determine optimal anticoagulation intensity and timing, balancing thrombosis prevention with bleeding risk in this fragile patient group. This study has several limitations. Its retrospective design introduces potential for selection bias and unmeasured confounding. The analysis was performed at a single high-volume transplant center, which may limit generalizability to other institutions with different VV-ECMO practices or anticoagulation protocols. Duplex ultrasonography was not performed uniformly across all patients, raising the possibility of underdiagnosis of asymptomatic DVT. In addition, surveillance bias is possible, because VV-ECMO–bridged or otherwise higher-acuity patients may have been more likely to undergo diagnostic imaging, potentially increasing DVT detection independent of true incidence. Because the frequency of duplex ultrasonography was not available in a standardized manner, we were unable to quantify imaging intensity by subgroup, and this limitation should be considered when interpreting group comparisons. Additionally, information on long-term anticoagulation adherence and PE severity was limited. Because anticoagulation exposure was analyzed largely as a binary variable, our findings may be subject to time-dependent confounding and reverse causation if anticoagulation was initiated in response to evolving clinical suspicion or diagnosis of thromboembolic events; therefore, the observed association between anticoagulation and PE should not be interpreted as causal. Although case-level review in the VV-ECMO–bridged cohort confirmed that anticoagulation preceded PE diagnosis, residual time-dependent bias cannot be excluded in the overall cohort. Nonetheless, the large sample size, standardized institutional protocols, and long follow-up period strengthen the validity of our findings. Conclusion In summary, post-transplant DVT represents a frequent and clinically significant complication among lung transplant recipients, particularly those bridged with VV-ECMO. DVT is associated with increased postoperative morbidity, prolonged hospitalization, and reduced survival. Preoperative VV-ECMO support identifies a subgroup with higher hemostatic complexity and greater susceptibility to thromboembolic events. Our findings highlight the need for vigilant DVT surveillance and optimization of perioperative anticoagulation strategies to improve post-transplant outcomes in this high-risk population. chunks.content: Introduction Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) is a systemic autoimmune disorder that is defined by arterial, venous, or microvascular thrombosis, pregnancy morbidity, and nonthrombotic manifestations, such as thrombocytopenia and valvular heart disease. , APS is characterized by persistent positivity for antiphospholipid (aPL) antibodies, including anticardiolipin antibodies, anti–β2-glycoprotein I (aβ2GPI) antibodies, and the lupus anticoagulant (LA). Venous thromboembolism (VTE), including deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE), is the most frequent initial clinical manifestation. Arterial thromboembolism (ATE) is less common, and catastrophic APS (CAPS) is rare. , , Both are associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. Long-term anticoagulation is the cornerstone of therapy for thrombotic APS. Most patients are treated with vitamin K antagonists (VKAs), particularly warfarin, because of their established efficacy in preventing recurrent thrombosis. However, VKAs present unique challenges in the perioperative setting given their long half-life (∼40 hours) and slow re-establishment of therapeutic anticoagulation, which can lead to 1 to 2 weeks of subtherapeutic anticoagulation during planned interruptions. Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are increasingly prescribed, but randomized trials and meta-analyses show that DOACs are inferior to VKAs in high-risk APS, particularly in triple-positive patients. , , , Perioperative management of anticoagulation in APS is challenging. APS is recognized as a high-risk thrombotic condition, and minimizing perioperative recurrent VTE and ATE during interruption of antithrombotic therapy is a clinical priority. , Bridging anticoagulation with low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) can be used to mitigate the perioperative risk for thrombosis; however, data from both randomized controlled trials and observational studies of patients without APS suggest that bridging increases postoperative bleeding without clearly reducing perioperative thromboembolism. , , Additional perioperative challenges in patients with APS include the use of concomitant antiplatelet therapy, higher international normalized ratio (INR) targets in recurrent thrombosis, coexisting immune thrombocytopenia, and the perceived risk for CAPS with periprocedural anticoagulation withdrawal and associated surgical stress, all of which further complicate decision-making. , , , , Despite these complexities, the current guidelines, including those of the American College of Chest Physicians (ACCP) and the European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology, recognize APS as a high-risk condition that warrants individualized perioperative management. , However, these recommendations are based mainly on expert opinion and extrapolation from non-APS populations. There are limited data that describe the perioperative management of antithrombotic therapy for patients with thrombotic APS. The efficacy and safety of the current perioperative anticoagulation management practices in patients with APS are not known. To address these important knowledge gaps, we conducted a single-center, retrospective cohort study to evaluate the risks for postoperative thromboembolism and bleeding after perioperative interruption of anticoagulation in patients with thrombotic APS who underwent planned surgical procedures. Methods Study population We conducted a single-center, retrospective cohort study of anticoagulated patients with thrombotic APS who underwent periprocedural anticoagulation management for planned surgery between 1 January 2016 and 14 April 2025. Patients were identified using a screening roster of all consecutive patients who underwent perioperative assessment for anticoagulation interruption at The Ottawa Hospital (TOH)’s Thrombosis Clinic and a list of filter functions that limited the screening list to patients with any previous documented APS test results conducted at TOH. Filtered outpatient perioperative visits at the TOH Thrombosis Clinic were screened for eligibility. Patients were included if they were ≥18 years of age, had a diagnosis of thrombotic APS (primary or secondary), and were prescribed anticoagulation with a VKA, DOAC, or LMWH. The diagnosis of APS was made by the managing thrombosis physician and was confirmed during record review based on the revised 2006 Sapporo classification criteria, requiring (1) documentation of arterial, venous, or microvascular thrombotic events, and (2) a clinically relevant aPL profile defined as persistently positive LA, anticardiolipin (aCL immunoglobulin G [IgG]/IgM), or aβ2GPI IgG/IgM antibodies, confirmed on ≥2 occasions at least 12 weeks apart. , Eligibility was determined using the 2006 Revised Sapporo Criteria because of the anticipated difficulties in retrospectively classifying patients using the 2023 American College of Rheumatology (ACR)/European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology criteria. Patients with microvascular thrombotic manifestations were included if the treating clinician documented the event as likely attributable to thrombotic APS pathophysiology. Patients who concurrently received antiplatelet therapy or those with advanced chronic kidney disease (creatinine clearance <30 mL/min or on dialysis) were also included. A planned procedure was defined as a surgery/procedure that occurred ≥72 hours from the decision that a surgical/procedural intervention was needed. Patients were excluded if (1) they had isolated obstetric APS without vascular thrombosis, (2) they underwent a minor procedure that was deemed safe to perform without interrupting anticoagulation therapy (eg, minimal bleeding risk procedures ), (3) they had inadequate documentation regarding the perioperative anticoagulation management, (4) the planned procedure was cancelled, (5) the procedure was emergent/unplanned (<72 hours from decision to intervene), or (6) the patient was pregnant at the time of perioperative interruption. aPL antibody assays aPL testing

A planned procedure was defined as a surgery/procedure that occurred ≥72 hours from the decision that a surgical/procedural intervention was needed. Patients were excluded if (1) they had isolated obstetric APS without vascular thrombosis, (2) they underwent a minor procedure that was deemed safe to perform without interrupting anticoagulation therapy (eg, minimal bleeding risk procedures ), (3) they had inadequate documentation regarding the perioperative anticoagulation management, (4) the planned procedure was cancelled, (5) the procedure was emergent/unplanned (<72 hours from decision to intervene), or (6) the patient was pregnant at the time of perioperative interruption. aPL antibody assays aPL testing at the Eastern Ontario Regional Laboratory Association was performed using the Bio-Rad enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) platform (Bio-Rad Laboratories, Hercules, CA) before 2018. From 2018 onward, Eastern Ontario Regional Laboratory Association transitioned to the BioFlash chemiluminescent immunoassay (CLIA) platform (Inova Diagnostics, San Diego, CA). Both systems were used to detect aCL IgG/IgM and aβ2GPI IgG/IgM antibodies. The antibody titers were considered positive for both ELISA and CLIA when the values exceeded a nonparametric 99th percentile threshold that was established using a reference population of healthy individuals in accordance with international consensus criteria for APS classification and testing for aPL with solid-phase assays. , This 99th percentile threshold corresponded to a titer of ≥20 GPL/MPL units for ELISA and ≥20 chemiluminescent units for CLIA. LA screening was performed using a lupus-sensitive activated partial thromboplastin time (LA-sensitive aPTT) assay (PTT-SP; Instrumentation Laboratory, Bedford, MA) and a dilute Russell’s viper venom time assay (LaCHECK; Precision BioLogic, Dartmouth, NS, Canada) using a Siemens CS-2100 analyzer. LA confirmation was performed using a dilute Russell’s viper venom time-based confirmatory assay with excess phospholipid (LaSure; Precision BioLogic, Dartmouth, NS, Canada). Conversion thresholds that were established by the International Society on Thrombosis and Haemostasis (ISTH) Scientific and Standardization Committee on Lupus Anticoagulant/Antiphospholipid Antibodies were used to harmonize the semiquantitative interpretation of titer values across the ELISA and CLIA platforms. The aPL titers were categorized as low, moderate, or high using these thresholds ( ). Perioperative anticoagulation management Perioperative anticoagulation management was carried out according to local practice at the TOH Thrombosis Clinic in accordance with contemporary clinical practice guidelines. , Decisions on periprocedural anticoagulation management were made by the treating physician. Procedural bleed risk classification was determined post hoc as minimal bleed risk, low/moderate bleed risk, or high bleed risk based on physician assessment and consistent with the ISTH procedural bleed risk stratification. VKAs were discontinued 5 days before the planned procedure and resumed on the evening of the procedure (postoperative day 0). VKAs were usually resumed using a postoperative loading dose (typically double the maintenance VKA dose for 2 days) at the discretion of the treating physician. , Preoperative INR testing was routinely performed on the day before surgery, and oral vitamin K was administered to patients with an INR >1.5. The decision to use bridging anticoagulation with LMWH was at the treating physician's discretion; LMWH bridging practices typically aligned with clinical practice guideline recommendations. DOACs were interrupted according to the ACCP clinical practice guideline recommendations and Thrombosis Canada guidance, , which are consistent with the approach used in the PAUSE study. DOACs were typically interrupted 1 day before low/moderate bleed–risk procedures and 2 days before high bleed–risk procedures with no dose given on the day of surgery. DOACs were resumed ∼24 hours after low/moderate bleed–risk procedures and 48 to 72 hours after high bleed–risk procedures. Study outcomes The primary outcomes were the 30-day postoperative risks of (1) ATE, (2) VTE, and (3) major bleeding. ATE included ischemic stroke, transient ischemic attack (TIA), and systemic embolism; VTE included pulmonary embolism and DVT (definitions are provided in ). Major bleeding was defined according to the ISTH surgical major bleeding criteria. Secondary outcomes included the 30-day postoperative risks for clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding (CRNMB), microvascular thrombotic events, CAPS, and all-cause mortality. CRNMB was defined according to the ISTH criteria. Microvascular thrombotic events were defined as new or recurrent small-vessel manifestations that were attributable to thrombotic APS pathophysiology (eg, digital ischemia and renal thrombotic microangiopathy), as determined by the treating physician and verified by chart review. CAPS was defined according to international consensus criteria. Outcomes were adjudicated in duplicate (M.P., J.R.S.) and were assessed for 30 days following the date of procedure, up to the study end date of April 14 th , 2025. Statistical analysis Demographic and aPL characteristics were summarized on a per-patient basis, whereas procedural and clinical outcome data were analyzed on a per-interruption basis. For patients who underwent >1 perioperative interruption within 30 days, outcomes were measured leading up to the second procedure, and outcomes were then ascertained for 30 days following the second procedure. If multiple procedures occurred consecutively during the same perioperative interruption, the outcomes were ascertained for 30 days following the last procedure

Statistical analysis Demographic and aPL characteristics were summarized on a per-patient basis, whereas procedural and clinical outcome data were analyzed on a per-interruption basis. For patients who underwent >1 perioperative interruption within 30 days, outcomes were measured leading up to the second procedure, and outcomes were then ascertained for 30 days following the second procedure. If multiple procedures occurred consecutively during the same perioperative interruption, the outcomes were ascertained for 30 days following the last procedure in that interruption period. Categorical variables were summarized as counts and proportions. Continuous variables were summarized as means with standard deviations (SDs) for normally distributed data or medians with interquartile ranges (IQRs) for nonnormally distributed data. Exploratory analyses were performed to evaluate procedural and clinical predictors of perioperative bridging use patterns and postoperative bleeding. Each perioperative interruption was analyzed as a distinct clinical episode, and generalized estimating equations (GEE) with a binomial family, a logit link, a robust sandwich variance estimator, and an independence working correlation structure were used to account for within-patient clustering. Given the limited number of postoperative bleeding events, associations between ISTH procedural bleed risk stratification (minimal/low/moderate vs high), urologic or gynecologic procedures (vs all other procedures), and postoperative bleeding were assessed using separate univariable GEE models. In contrast, associations between triple-positive APS status, previous ATE, and receipt of any therapeutic-dose LMWH bridging among VKA-treated patients were examined using a multivariable GEE model (because of an adequate number of bridging exposures). For paired comparisons of preoperative and postoperative bridging intensity, the analyses were limited to VKA-treated patients who received preoperative bridging, and McNemar’s test was used to evaluate changes in preoperative bridging dosing to postoperative dosing. The results are presented as odds ratios (ORs) with corresponding 95% confidence intervals (95% CIs); statistical significance was defined as P < .05. All analyses were exploratory and not adjusted for multiplicity. The 30-day risks for clinical outcomes were reported as proportions with corresponding 95% CIs, calculated using exact methods (Clopper-Pearson). All statistical analyses were performed using Microsoft Excel (version 2511) and R Statistical Software (R Core Team 2025 v4.5.2; R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria). Ethical approval for this study was granted by the Ottawa Health Sciences Research Ethics Board. This study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Results Study population and procedure types A total of 1792 perioperative encounters were screened for eligibility between January 2016 and April 2025 ( ), and of those, 172 patients who underwent 282 perioperative interruptions met the criteria for inclusion in the analysis. The mean ± SD age of the cohort was 59.7 ± 13.9 years ( ), and a majority of patients were female (n = 98; 57.0%). Most patients were anticoagulated with VKAs (n = 146; 84.9%); a small proportion were prescribed a DOAC (n = 25; 14.5%). Most patients had a target INR of 2.0 to 3.0 (93.9%), whereas a minority were maintained at a higher therapeutic range of 2.5 to 3.5 (4.9%). The mean ± SD CHA 2 DS 2 -Va score (congestive heart failure, hypertension, age, diabetes, prior stroke/TIA or systemic arterial embolism, vascular disease) in patients with atrial fibrillation was 4.4 ± 1.4. Advanced chronic kidney disease (creatinine clearance <30 mL/min or dialysis) was present in 5.2% of patients, and 4 (2.3%) were on dialysis. Most procedures were performed on an outpatient basis (n = 245; 86.9%), and 112 (39.8%) interruptions were classified as high bleed–risk procedures ( ). Ultrasound-guided renal biopsies accounted for 11.0% (n = 31) of all perioperative interruptions. Twenty patients (7.1%) had thrombocytopenia (platelet count <100 × 10 9 /L) within the 6 months before surgery, and 12 patients (4.3%) had thrombocytopenia at the time of surgery. One patient (0.3%) had documented ISTH-defined major bleeding, and 11 (3.9%) had thromboembolism within the 6 months before surgery. aPL testing More than half of the patients had a history of VTE (n = 118; 68.6%) and/or ATE (n = 87; 50.6%). Few patients had documented previous noncriteria manifestations of APS (n = 43; 25.0%), and 12 (7.0%) had a history of Libman-Sacks endocarditis. aPL positivity and the Miyakis classification profiles are outlined in . A total of 53 patients (30.8%) had a concurrent autoimmune disease, including 39 with a diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus (22.7%). A total of 53 patients (30.8%) had a concurrent autoimmune disease, including 39 with a diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus (22.7%). Perioperative anticoagulation management VKAs were discontinued for 5 days preoperatively (last dose on postoperative day [POD] ˗6) in nearly all interruptions (95.4%; ). VKAs were resumed in the evening on the day of surgery in most patients (median, POD 0; IQR, POD 0-1). Most (81.2%) restarted on POD 0, and 16.1% resumed on POD 1. A total of 21 patients (7.4%) had a preoperative INR of ≥1.5, and preoperative vitamin K was required in 3.2% of interruptions because of INR ≥1.5 on POD ˗1. Warfarin was resumed using a postoperative loading dose in 102 (43.2%) interruptions. For DOAC-treated patients ( ), the median duration of preoperative interruption was 72 hours (IQR, 60-72) for high bleed–risk procedures and 48 hours (IQR, 42-66) for minimal/low/moderate bleed–risk procedures. Postoperative DOAC resumption occurred at a median of 60 hours (IQR, 36-72) after high bleed–risk procedures and 36 hours (IQR, 36-36) after minimal/low/moderate bleed–risk procedures. Concurrent antiplatelet therapy was documented in 12.7% of interruptions; antiplatelet agents were continued in more than half of the interruptions that involved antiplatelet-treated patients (58.3%). Bridging practices among VKA-treated patients are summarized in . In terms of preoperative bridging, 90 interruptions (42.9%) involved any therapeutic-dose LMWH bridging, whereas 77 (36.7%) involved prophylactic-dose bridging and 43 (20.5%) involved no bridging. Among VKA-treated patients who received any preoperative bridging (n = 188), 35.1% received therapeutic-dose bridging preoperatively and were transitioned to prophylactic-dose postoperatively (i.e., de-escalation). Otherwise, 43.6% maintained prophylactic dosing from before to after the procedure. Only 0.5% escalated from prophylactic preoperative bridging to therapeutic intensity postoperatively, and 20.7% remained on therapeutic bridging throughout. A pairwise analysis demonstrated significantly higher odds of de-escalating bridging postoperatively (McNemar paired OR, 66.0; 95% CI, 9.1-500.0; P < .0001), reflecting substantially more transitions from preoperative therapeutic-dose bridging to postoperative prophylactic bridging (or no bridging) than the reverse. Triple-positive patients were more likely to have received any therapeutic-dose bridging therapy than those who did not have triple positivity (72.2% vs 30.0%; OR, 7.6; 95% CI, 3.2-18.2; P < .001). Similarly, therapeutic bridging was more commonly administered for patients with a history of ATE than for those without a previous ATE (53.1% vs 27.4%; OR, 3.4; 95% CI, 1.5-7.8; P = .003). Clinical outcomes There were 2 postoperative ATEs, yielding a 30-day postoperative ATE risk of 0.7% (95% CI, 0.2-2.6). The first event was a TIA on POD 13 after an umbilical hernia repair (54-year-old male on warfarin, INR target of 2.0 to 3.0, no concurrent ASA, aCL positive, history of recurrent stroke/TIA) that occurred despite resuming warfarin using a loading dose and receiving postoperative LMWH prophylaxis (dalteparin 5000 IU subcutaneous [SQ] once daily until INR > 2.0; INR was 3.4 at presentation with TIA). The second event was a systemic embolism (right superficial femoral artery) on POD 2 after a facet injection (59-year-old male on warfarin, INR target of 2.0 to 3.0, taking 325 mg ASA daily, aCL positive, history of TIA) requiring catheter-directed thrombolysis on POD 5. This occurred despite resuming warfarin with a loading dose, receiving postoperative LMWH prophylaxis (dalteparin 5000 IU SQ once daily until INR > 2.0), and aspirin 325 mg daily starting on POD 1. There was 1 central line–associated upper extremity DVT (0.4%; 95% CI, 0.1-2.0) that occurred on POD 10. There were 2 major bleeding events during the 30-day follow-up period, yielding a 30-day major bleeding risk of 0.7% (95% CI, 0.2-2.6; ). Both occurred in patients who underwent high bleed–risk procedures. The first event occurred following a kidney biopsy in a patient on warfarin (preoperative INR = 1.1, no concurrent antiplatelet therapy), which led to a perinephric hematoma with interval expansion on repeat ultrasound and an associated drop in hemoglobin of >20 g/L. The second event was fatal and occurred in a 46-year-old female (aCL positive, previous recurrent VTE, thrombocytopenia) following a right hemipelvectomy (high bleed–risk procedure; estimated blood loss 3.5 L) owing to nonmetastatic myxofibrosarcoma. The patient (warfarin at baseline, bridging with prophylactic fondaparinux owing to a history of injection reaction to LMWH) developed iliac artery rupture with massive bleeding on POD 8, requiring activation of a massive transfusion protocol and leading to immediate pulseless electrical activity (PEA) arrest. Despite urgent vessel ligation, right lower-limb amputation, and massive transfusion, the patient developed multiorgan failure and died

The patient (warfarin at baseline, bridging with prophylactic fondaparinux owing to a history of injection reaction to LMWH) developed iliac artery rupture with massive bleeding on POD 8, requiring activation of a massive transfusion protocol and leading to immediate pulseless electrical activity (PEA) arrest. Despite urgent vessel ligation, right lower-limb amputation, and massive transfusion, the patient developed multiorgan failure and died on POD 17. There were 9 CRNMB events ( ), corresponding to a 30-day risk of 3.2% (95% CI, 1.7-6.0). Eight events occurred in patients who were anticoagulated with warfarin, and 1 occurred in a patient who was treated with rivaroxaban. High bleed–risk surgery (vs minimal/low/moderate) was associated with significantly greater odds of postoperative bleeding (composite of major bleeding + CRNMB: OR, 7.3; 95% CI, 1.5-35.4; P = .01). Similarly, undergoing a urologic or gynecologic procedure (vs all others) was also associated with substantially increased odds of postoperative bleeding (OR, 6.6; 95% CI, 1.8-24.5; P = .005). Postoperative microvascular APS occurred in 2 patients (0.7%; 95% CI, 0.2-2.6). The first occurred on POD 10 in a triple-positive patient who developed biopsy-proven thrombotic microangiopathy of a transplanted kidney, which led to graft rejection. The second happened on POD 8 in another triple-positive patient and presented as an adrenal gland hemorrhage. Clinicians attributed this event to microvascular thrombosis and adrenal infarction, which subsequently led to adrenal insufficiency. This occurred in a 25-year-old triple-positive APS patient with ulcerative colitis who underwent a colonoscopy. On POD 8, the patient developed acalculous cholecystitis, adrenal hemorrhage, and thrombocytopenia while receiving prophylactic tinzaparin at a dose of 4500 IU SQ daily. A heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) ELISA was positive (optical density OD, 1.6), but functional testing (serotonin release assay) was negative, confirming the absence of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. This single event met the criteria for probable CAPS (0.4%; 95% CI, 0.1-2.0), corresponding to a 30-day risk of 1.4% (95% CI, 0.0-7.6) among triple-positive patients. There was 1 death during the 30-day follow-up (0.4%; 95% CI, 0.1-2.0) that was attributed to fatal bleeding (outlined earlier). Discussion Data to guide the perioperative management of antithrombotic therapy for patients with thrombotic APS are limited. Herein, we report results from a single-center, retrospective cohort of anticoagulated adults with thrombotic APS who underwent a planned invasive procedure or surgery. Perioperative anticoagulation management was generally consistent with contemporary guideline-directed practice. The 30-day risks for ATE, VTE, and ISTH-defined major bleeding were low and comparable with contemporary non-APS cohorts. CAPS, a recognized concern in the setting of anticoagulation withdrawal and surgical stress, was rare. Our findings suggest that contemporary perioperative anticoagulation strategies, when applied with individualized attention to thrombotic and bleeding risk, can be safely implemented in patients with APS. Perioperative management in our cohort followed a consistent framework that reflected both guideline-concordant practices and local practice patterns. Most VKA-treated patients received some form of parenteral bridging anticoagulation, reflecting the ACCP guideline designation of APS as a high thrombotic–risk condition for which bridging may be appropriate. Concurrent antiplatelet therapy was uncommon (∼13%), and complicating perioperative thrombocytopenia was rare (4.3%). Few patients had a higher INR target (2.5-3.5; ∼5%). Holding warfarin for 5 days before surgery led to INR normalization (INR < 1.5) in most (∼92.6%) VKA-treated patients. In a previous single-center APS surgical cohort, guideline-concordant periprocedural anticoagulation management was associated with fewer thrombotic and hemorrhagic complications (7% vs 33%; OR, 0.14; 95% CI, 0.02-0.81; P = .04), and an INR of ≤1.5 at surgery was associated with fewer major bleeding events (6% vs 29%; OR, 0.19; 95% CI, 0.02-0.98; P = .05). The 30-day risks for major bleeding (0.7%; 95% CI, 0.2-2.6) and CRNMB (3.2%; 95% CI, 1.7-6.0) compared favorably with those of contemporary non-APS cohorts. The 30-day risks for major bleeding in the BRIDGE trial were 1.3% and 3.2% in the nonbridging and bridging arms, respectively, whereas the risks ranged from 0.9% to 1.9% in the PAUSE study depending on the DOAC in question. , Importantly, in our study, major bleeding events were attributed to anatomic and procedural factors rather than anticoagulation status at bleeding onset. Most bleeding events occurred after a high bleed–risk procedure, including both of the recorded major bleeding events, and more than half of the bleeding events involved urologic or gynecologic procedures (renal biopsy, hysterectomy, transurethral resection of bladder tumor, uterine ablation). Few early bleeding events occurred during therapeutic-dose bridging; most occurred after appropriate perioperative interruption with INR values within the expected range at surgery. In contrast, delayed CRNMB events typically occurred after discontinuation of bridging during warfarin therapy with INRs within the therapeutic range (ie, not supratherapeutic), suggesting that these

anatomic and procedural factors rather than anticoagulation status at bleeding onset. Most bleeding events occurred after a high bleed–risk procedure, including both of the recorded major bleeding events, and more than half of the bleeding events involved urologic or gynecologic procedures (renal biopsy, hysterectomy, transurethral resection of bladder tumor, uterine ablation). Few early bleeding events occurred during therapeutic-dose bridging; most occurred after appropriate perioperative interruption with INR values within the expected range at surgery. In contrast, delayed CRNMB events typically occurred after discontinuation of bridging during warfarin therapy with INRs within the therapeutic range (ie, not supratherapeutic), suggesting that these delayed events were not directly attributable to bridging. Taken together, these findings underscore the importance of carefully considering the type of procedure (eg, urologic procedures) and postoperative bleeding risk when devising a perioperative anticoagulation management plan. Data from non-APS populations indicate that bridging increases postoperative bleeding without clearly reducing the thromboembolism risk, but these studies enrolled patients with lower-risk indications (eg, atrial fibrillation) and may not be generalizable to APS. , APS is both clinically and biologically heterogeneous. More than half of our cohort met Miyakis category I criteria, one-quarter were triple-positive, and moderate to high aPL titers were observed across multiple isotypes. These features typically indicate a higher thrombotic risk. Our cohort also demonstrated a substantial burden of clinical thrombotic risk factors. More than half had a previous ATE, the majority had a history of VTE, and nearly one-third had a concurrent autoimmune disease. Clinicians seemed to incorporate APS-related thrombotic risk into their perioperative decision-making. Patients with triple-positive APS and those with a previous ATE were more likely to receive therapeutic-dose LMWH bridging. Our findings suggest that a one-size-fits-all approach is unlikely to be appropriate in APS. Tailoring perioperative anticoagulation management to both APS-related thrombotic risk and procedural bleed risk seems to have been both feasible and safe in this heterogeneous, higher-risk cohort. Postoperative bridging in our cohort frequently comprised prophylactic-dose LMWH after high bleed–risk procedures; this may, in part, represent local extrapolation of postoperative dose modulation concepts that have been evaluated in other high thrombotic–risk populations (eg, patients with a mechanical heart valve), recognizing that therapeutic-dose anticoagulation in the immediate postoperative period is a shared driver of major bleeding risk. Given the observational design and low event counts, this practice pattern should be interpreted cautiously. Both ATE events occurred while patients were receiving postoperative LMWH prophylaxis. Microvascular events were uncommon overall (0.7%) but occurred exclusively in triple-positive patients; 1 event met the criteria for probable CAPS, which happened while the patient was receiving postoperative prophylactic LMWH. Although definitive causal inferences cannot be made, these observations, together with published case reports describing rapid, severe thrombotic events in triple-positive secondary APS (often with concomitant systemic autoimmune disease) after brief warfarin interruption despite LMWH bridging, supports considering therapeutic-dose bridging and tightly timed periprocedural anticoagulation strategies that minimize time off anticoagulation in the highest-risk phenotypes (ie, triple-positive APS and/or previous ATE). Conversely, for lower-risk phenotypes and/or higher bleed–risk procedures, initiating prophylactic-intensity anticoagulation early in the postoperative period with escalation as surgical hemostasis permits may offer a pragmatic balance. Prospective studies are needed to confirm optimal strategies across APS phenotypes. This study has several strengths. To our knowledge, it represents the largest, single-center cohort that evaluated perioperative anticoagulation management in patients with thrombotic APS. Perioperative antithrombotic strategies at our center followed relatively standardized workflows, enabling detailed characterization of warfarin interruption intervals, preoperative INR assessment, vitamin K use, LMWH bridging dose and timing, and postoperative VKA resumption practices. The outcome definitions adhered to widely recognized international standards, and the cohort encompassed a broad mix of invasive procedures with more than one-third classified as high bleed–risk procedures. TOH is the regional referral center for thrombosis, APS, and stroke, and patients with APS undergo close, frequent monitoring, including regular pharmacist-specialist contacts for VKA management. Consequently, although retrospective analyses are inherently susceptible to variable documentation and information bias, the likelihood of missing major thrombotic or bleeding outcomes is low. Important limitations should also be acknowledged. First, the measurement of aPL antibodies is itself a known challenge; our cohort spanned a period during which laboratory methodology transitioned from ELISA to CLIA platforms. Although we harmonized titers using published ISTH conversion thresholds and applied a 99th percentile positivity cutoff, some misclassification remains possible. Second, several patients underwent multiple perioperative interruptions, which led to more interruptions than there were patients. Although GEE models were used to account for within-patient clustering when evaluating bridging patterns and overall bleeding risk, events were too few to support multivariable modelling of clinical outcomes. Thus, the determined estimates and their CIs should be interpreted cautiously. Third, serial postoperative INR trajectories were not uniformly available across interruption episodes, precluding estimation of time spent below therapeutic range and time to reattain a therapeutic INR after warfarin resumption.

Second, several patients underwent multiple perioperative interruptions, which led to more interruptions than there were patients. Although GEE models were used to account for within-patient clustering when evaluating bridging patterns and overall bleeding risk, events were too few to support multivariable modelling of clinical outcomes. Thus, the determined estimates and their CIs should be interpreted cautiously. Third, serial postoperative INR trajectories were not uniformly available across interruption episodes, precluding estimation of time spent below therapeutic range and time to reattain a therapeutic INR after warfarin resumption. Fourth, concomitant hydroxychloroquine use was not systematically captured, limiting assessment of its potential influence on perioperative thrombotic and bleeding outcomes. Finally, as a retrospective, single-center analysis, perioperative decisions, including bridging intensity, were not protocolized and event counts were low, leading to wide confidence intervals for the event estimates. In summary, patients with thrombotic APS who underwent planned interruption of anticoagulation at our center experienced low 30-day risks for ATE, VTE, and major bleeding when managed using contemporary perioperative strategies. Clinical practice patterns reflected a risk-adapted approach. Clinicians used therapeutic-dose LMWH bridging more often in patients with triple-positive APS or a history of ATE. They used prophylactic-dose bridging more frequently after high bleed–risk procedures. Individualized management that integrates APS-related thrombotic risk, procedural bleed risk, and clinical context seems safe. The occurrence of microvascular APS manifestations, including 1 case of probable CAPS, underscores that high-risk phenotypes remain vulnerable during anticoagulation withdrawal and merit heightened vigilance. Future research should focus on multicenter prospective studies to refine risk stratification, define optimal bridging strategies across APS phenotypes, and better characterize clinical outcomes in the perioperative setting.
